title: five disguises, one promise
hook: the forest years are over, and to keep their word, five brothers and Draupadi must vanish for a year
carry: satya: keep your word, even when it humbles you

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dharma, the voice at the lake, revealed as Yudhishthira's own father, after a choice that put not being cruel above gain. Your line was dharma puts non-cruelty above gain.

One last year, lived among people, without being recognized. Those were the terms of the dice game, and if anyone sees through them, the exile begins again. So the five brothers and Draupadi sit together, and Yudhishthira asks each of them a question. Not where will you hide. What will you be? Where will you work, and as whom? They have chosen a kingdom to vanish into: the land of the Matsyas, ruled by King Virata. The Virata book opens with something close to a job interview, held in secret.
screen: `ONE YEAR, UNRECOGNIZED.` → `WHAT WILL YOU BE?` → `THE COURT OF KING VIRATA.`

segments.voice: Why go through with it at all? In the forest, Bhima begged Yudhishthira more than once to stop waiting and fight; the dice game was rigged. And Yudhishthira said no. I gave my word. That's the teaching under this whole year, and Hindus have a word for it: satya, truth, which includes the promise kept. In the stories Hindu families grow up on, King Harishchandra gives up his kingdom rather than break his word, and Rama goes to the forest so his father's promise stands. The Pandavas belong to that line. So listen to the answers. Yudhishthira will be Kanka, a Brahmin who plays dice with the king. The man whose love of dice cost them everything wears it as his cover. Bhima will be Vallava, the cook. Arjuna will hide his bowstring scars under bangles and live as Brihannala, who teaches dance to the palace women. Nakula will keep the horses, Sahadeva the cattle. And Draupadi, a queen, will serve a queen as Sairandhri, a maid who dresses hair. Their priest Dhaumya gives them rules for a king's house: don't take a seat that might be someone else's, speak when you're asked, don't show off. Princes become staff for a year, to keep a promise made to people who cheated them. Today, satya rarely costs a throne. It looks like the promise you made when it was easy, kept when it's embarrassing. In Hindu teaching, a word given is part of dharma.
screen: `I GAVE MY WORD: SATYA.` · `KEPT PROMISES, AND KANKA THE DICER.` · `A COOK, A DANCE TEACHER, A MAID.` · then, large: `PRINCES BECOME STAFF.`

segments.voice: Hindus often begin a puja or a vow with a sankalpa, a stated resolve. Choose one small promise you can truly keep today, something you already owe someone. Some hold a little water in the right palm as they say it. Say it once, silently and plainly, and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, you can make it in your prayer; if you don't, simply say it to yourself.
Virata. The king of the Matsyas, whose court will hide the Pandavas and Draupadi for their year in disguise.
Your line: satya, keep your word, even when it humbles you. A dice player, a cook, a dance teacher, two herders and a maid. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 807 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WEAPONS IN THE SHAMI TREE.`

howItsDone: Retellings of the Virata book keep the disguise names (Kanka, Vallava, Brihannala, Sairandhri), and the year in hiding is told as a promise kept to the letter; Harishchandra and Rama are the stories Hindu families most often tell about keeping one's word.

Virata.meaning: king of the Matsyas, in whose court the Pandavas hide

Kanka.meaning: Yudhishthira's disguise: a Brahmin who plays dice with the king

Brihannala.meaning: Arjuna's disguise: a dance teacher for the palace women

Sairandhri.meaning: Draupadi's disguise: a maid who dresses the queen's hair

Dhaumya.meaning: the Pandavas' family priest, who advises them on life at court

the one cloth Nala and Damayanti shared

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Pandava-pravesa), the Pandavas choose their disguises and Dhaumya's counsel on living in a king's household
Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Bhima urges Yudhishthira to fight before the term ends, and Yudhishthira refuses because of his pledge

Markandeya Purana, the story of Harishchandra, who gives up his kingdom to keep his word
